name: GlobalLogic
description: Two stacks of metallic cards animated with a custom diagonal-bend vertex shader. The cards flex in a synchronized wave while the camera orbits with variable speed. Dramatic orange and red point lights create depth against a white fog background.
reason: This project was created for GlobalLogic to showcase their brand in a visually engaging way instead of a static image.

name: N-IX Branding Live Background
description: A visualization of 1,000 metallic spheres (InstancedMesh) that morph between seven geometric shapes — circle, cube, sphere, Perlin-noise terrain, and DNA helix. Features a live procedural background shader with an animated studio hotspot, orbiting colored lights, per-sphere blinking, and full GUI controls for animation, material, and camera.
reason: On the N-IX website, was used 512 images in the dom! To make animation more efficient, I created a live background with 1,000 spheres that morph between seven geometric shapes. The background is procedurally generated and animated in real-time.

name: Live Background for any Card
description: A full landing page where a single fixed WebGL canvas renders live backgrounds inside every card simultaneously using scissor testing — one draw call per card, zero DOM canvases. Each card gets its own coordinate space via uBlockOffset. The shader layers three effects: five slowly drifting bokeh blobs in cyan, blue, and purple; a grid of twinkling static sparkles with per-cell random phase and speed; and 240 perspective-projected flying stars that cycle depth with fract() to create a continuous hyperspace zoom effect.
reason: A proof of concept for rendering rich animated backgrounds across an entire page with a single WebGL context — instead of one canvas per card, scissor testing lets the GPU clip the same shader to each card's bounding rect, keeping memory and overhead minimal.

name: GameInspire Tunnel Grid
description: Two curved dot-grid planes — one above and one below the camera — rendered as WebGL point sprites and scrolled toward the viewer in a continuous tunnel. A cylindrical bend compresses the X axis and a per-plane Y curvature arches the grids toward each other. The vertex shader handles perspective projection, near/far/edge alpha falloff, and a slow view-axis rotation. Top dots are cool blue, bottom dots are soft purple, both dimming as they approach the camera.
reason: Created for GameInspire to provide an immersive live background for their platform — a subtle infinite-tunnel animation in blue and purple tones that conveys depth and forward momentum without distracting from the content. On the site this element is a static image.

name: theMultiple Slot Drums
description: Three spinning slot-machine drums rendered entirely via ray marching signed distance functions — no geometry buffers. Each cylinder hosts six icon panels read from an SVG atlas, shaded with diffuse/specular lighting and glowing cyan torus rings that levitate around each drum. A fish-eye camera and a 10-second animation cycle featuring cubic ease-out deceleration snapping to sector boundaries give the piece a polished, tactile feel.
reason: Created for theMultiple to showcase their brand through an interactive slot-machine metaphor, combining custom SVG logos with geometric symbols on procedurally rendered 3D drums. They have animation on site but it based on image sequence. I created a real-time 3D version with ray marching and signed distance functions.

name: Reactive Particle Image
description: A PNG's alpha channel is sampled pixel-by-pixel to place a THREE.Points cloud, one particle per opaque pixel, colored with a scrolling HSL rainbow or a solid custom color. A raycaster tracks the mouse/touch position (auto-disabled after 150ms idle or on leaving the window) and gives nearby particles a velocity impulse, scattering them before they ease back to their origin coordinates. The whole field slowly rocks on two axes, and a GUI lets you swap in any image URL live.
reason: A personal practice sketch for learning raycasting against point clouds and building image-reveal effects out of particles instead of textures.

name: Particle Forms
description: A single WebGL point buffer holds two shapes at once — a golden-ratio-distributed sphere and a regular ground grid — distinguished per-vertex by an a_type attribute. The vertex shader displaces the sphere along its normals with 3D value noise and ripples the grid with a travelling sine wave modulated by noise, while a slow Y-axis rotation only affects the sphere. Perspective projection, point size, and alpha all fall off toward the grid's edges for depth. A GUI panel controls the background color and independently rebuilds the sphere and grid point counts live.
reason: A personal practice sketch for combining two differently shaped point clouds in a single draw call via a type attribute, and for wiring up GUI controls that safely tear down and rebuild WebGL buffers at runtime.

name: Braided Rope Live Background
description: Braided ropes, each built from strands twisting around a bent centerline, rendered entirely in a fragment shader with no geometry. Every pixel evaluates the strands and keeps only the closest one via a running best-depth comparison, so ropes correctly occlude each other and themselves as they twist. Two cheap analytic culls, a depth bound and a centerline-distance bound, skip whole strand loops per rope when they can't possibly win that pixel, without changing the output. A GUI panel exposes background color, a dynamic-vs-static camera angle, the rope bend amount, and live rope/strand counts, with the loops capped at compile-time max bounds and broken early to keep the GUI-driven counts within GLSL ES 1.00's constant-loop-bound requirement. A CSS title overlay sits on top with mix-blend-mode: difference so its color inverts against whatever ribbon color is animating underneath.
reason: A personal practice sketch for implementing per-pixel depth sorting, a mini painter's algorithm, inside a fragment shader with no real 3D geometry or depth buffer, and for finding cheap analytic bounds to cull work that can't affect the final pixel.

name: Fiberglass Light Bundle
description: A bundle of thin glass rods fans out from a single point below the frame and converges toward tips scattered within a circle around screen center, all rendered procedurally in a fragment shader with no geometry. Each rod gets a random pseudo-depth (thinner and dimmer the farther back it sits), its own random bend direction with a gentle wind-like sway, a glowing tip with a hot core and soft halo, fresnel rim and specular glass shading, and a couple of randomly placed flickering glints. Rod color can cycle per-strand through HSV over time or lock to a single static color. A cheap per-strand cull, checking distance to the unbent straight rod before paying for bend math, hue mixing, or glow falloffs, skips the expensive work for the many strands nowhere near a given pixel. The scene sits on a vignette background with soft drifting bokeh blobs and a radial fade to black at the edges, with a camera zoom/pan uniform layered on top so the whole composition can be reframed. A GUI panel exposes strand and bokeh counts, colors, fade radius, rod width, scatter radius, fresnel/specular intensity, and the camera controls.
reason: Inspired by a glowing fiber-optic bundle image on EPAM's website (epam.com) — I rebuilt the idea as a live procedural background instead of a static photo, with its own pseudo-3D depth, wind sway, and glass shading.
